metadata.file_name: McJames et al. (2023). Factors affecting teacher job satisfaction  a causal inference machine learning approach using data from TALIS 2018.pdf
metadata.title: Factors affecting teacher job satisfaction: a causal inference machine learning approach using data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the England subset of TALIS 2018, which is collected using a stratified two-stage probability sampling design within the country. Each teacher is assigned sampling weights, and the authors state that these sampling weights were fully accounted for in the analysis. They implement this using the Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) procedure described in the TALIS technical report (OECD, 2019b), which is consistent with replicate-weight variance estimation for complex survey designs. For missing data, they impute missing responses (see missing_data_handling) and then fit the causal BART models; the manuscript does not indicate any additional weight omission for the ML/causal estimation stage.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a TALIS teacher job satisfaction scale constructed from eight Likert items via confirmatory factor analysis, not a cognitive achievement score generated with PVs. Missing data handling is reported: the authors impute missing responses using missRanger, which is a single imputation approach, so PV-combining rules are not relevant to this outcome.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the England subset of TALIS 2018, restricting the full TALIS teacher sample to 2009 primary and 2376 lower secondary teachers (total n=4385). The analysis focuses on teacher job satisfaction measured from eight TALIS items and constructs binary treatment indicators (e.g., CPD participation, induction, mentoring, team teaching, observing, public school, class size threshold, out-of-field teaching, part-time contract). Missing responses in variables used in the study were imputed (missRanger) rather than deleting cases.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (England subset; primary & lower secondary teachers)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Causal BART (bartCause) ATEs with 95% confidence intervals: CPD ATE CI [0.035, 0.309]; Induction ATE CI [0.107, 0.329]; Team teaching ATE CI includes 0 (wide CI); Observing ATE CI includes 0 (wide CI); Part-time contract ATE = -0.216, 95% CI [-0.388, -0.044].
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (England subset; primary & lower secondary teachers) the study leveraged CPD participation (4+ events), induction participation, part-time contract (<90%), team teaching participation, and observing other teachers to estimate causal effects on teacher job satisfaction, finding that participation in continual professional development and induction activities had the most positive effects while part-time contracts had a negative effect. This indicates that school and system leaders should prioritize accessible CPD and induction supports and carefully review the job-security implications of part-time employment arrangements, while recognizing that causal identification relies on the study’s ignorability/overlap assumptions.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes the England subset of TALIS 2018, using 4,385 teachers (2,009 primary and 2,376 lower secondary) and a continuous teacher job satisfaction scale derived from eight Likert items. It estimates average treatment effects for multiple binary “treatments” (e.g., CPD participation, induction, mentoring, observing, team teaching, public school employment, class size ≥30, out-of-field teaching, and part-time contracts) using causal inference machine learning with BART via the R package bartCause, incorporating a propensity score as an additional predictor. Survey sampling weights are accounted for using Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR). Missing responses in analysis variables were imputed with missRanger (single imputation), and the authors note that imputation uncertainty is not fully captured in the main analysis. The strongest positive effects are for CPD (ATE CI [0.035, 0.309]) and induction (ATE CI [0.107, 0.329]), while part-time contracts reduce job satisfaction (ATE = -0.216, 95% CI [-0.388, -0.044]); other treatments show imprecise estimates with wide confidence intervals.
